When it refers to the tribe, it is not declined (diptotic), and when it refers to the group as a living entity, it is declined. As for "'Ad," since it has three letters with the middle one quiescent, it has no cause for non-declension in its first part, so it is declined.

"Al-taghiyah": Qatadah said its meaning is the cry that went beyond the limit of every cry. Some said the meaning is: because of the transgressing group. Others, among them Mujahid and Ibn Zayd, said the meaning is: because of the transgressing deed that they committed. Ibn Zayd also said something whose meaning is: "al-taghiyah" is a verbal noun like al-'aqibah, so it is as if He, Exalted is He, said: "because of their transgression." Abu 'Ubaydah also said this. This is strengthened by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Thamud denied by their transgression﴾ [al-Shams: 11]. The most correct and preferred of the opinions is the first, because it corresponds to what is mentioned concerning 'Ad, when it mentions the manner by which destruction occurred. According to the other opinions, the two matters do not correspond, because the transgression of Thamud is a cause, and the wind does not correspond to that, since it is not a cause of destruction but an instrument, just as the cry is.

"Al-sarsar" may be derived from "al-sirr" (cold), and this is the opinion of Qatadah. It may also be derived from "sarra al-shay'" when it made a sound. Some said the sound of the wind is "sarir," as if it imitates these two letters. "Al-'atiyah" means: the strong, the opposing. The wind rebelled against its keepers, opposing them, and it rebelled against the people of 'Ad by its severity. It is narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib and Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, that they said: "No drop of rain has ever descended from the sky except by a measure in the hand of an angel, and no wind has ever blown except in this way, except for the flood of Noah, peace be upon him, and the wind of 'Ad. God permitted these two to go out without the permission of the keepers."

[p. 386] "Taskhir" (subjugation) is the use of a thing with power over it. It is narrated that the wind began with them at dawn on Wednesday, eight days remaining in Shawwal, and it continued with them until the end of Wednesday, completing the month. "Husuman": Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, Qatadah, and Abu 'Ubaydah said its meaning is: complete, in succession, with nothing interrupting them. This is like the Arabs saying: "I did not meet him for a full year, a sinful one." The poet said:

"Remote ones that did not hear the lowing of a gathering,
and did not see a fire of a full, sinful year."

[p. 387] Al-Khalil said: that is, ill omen and misfortune. Ibn Zayd said: "husum" is the plural of "hasim," like "jalis" and "qa'id." Its meaning is that those days cut them off by destruction. From it comes "hasama al-'ilal" (he cut off the diseases), and from it "al-husam" (the sword). The pronoun in His saying, Exalted is He: "fiha sar'a" (lying prostrate in it) may refer to the nights and days, and it may refer to "their abode and their settlement," because the meaning of the statement requires it even though it is not spoken. Al-Tha'labi said: it is also said that it refers to the wind. The discussion of the comparison with the hollow trunks of palm trees has already been mentioned in the surah ﴿The Hour has drawn near﴾ [al-Qamar: 1]. "Al-khawiyah" means: fallen, whose trunks have become hollow through decay and corruption.

Then Exalted is He stopped at their matter with a stop for contemplation, saying, glorified is He: ﴿Do you see any remnant of them?﴾ The interpreters differed concerning "baqiyah" (remnant). Some, among them Ibn al-Anbari, said it is here an intensive form like 'allamah and nassabah, and the meaning is: "from one who remains." Ibn al-Anbari also said its meaning is: "from a remaining group." Others said "baqiyah" is a verbal noun, so the meaning is: "from survival."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 69, verses 9–17:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿And Pharaoh came, and those before him, and the overturned cities with sin.﴾ ﴿So they disobeyed the messenger of their Lord, and He seized them with a severe seizing.﴾ ﴿Indeed, when the water rose high, We carried you in the sailing ship.﴾ ﴿That We might make it for you a reminder, and that an attentive ear might retain it.﴾ ﴿Then when the Horn is blown with one blast.﴾ ﴿And the earth and the mountains are lifted and crushed with one crushing.﴾ ﴿So on that Day the Inevitable Event will occur.﴾ ﴿And the sky will split open, for it will be frail that Day.﴾ ﴿And the angels will be on its edges, and eight will bear above them, that Day, the Throne of your Lord.﴾

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Hamza, Abu Ja'far, Shayba, Abu 'Abd al-Rahman, and al-A'mash read: "wa-man qablahu" (وَمَن قَبْلَهُ) with a fatha on the qaf and a sukun on the ba', meaning the disbelieving nations who were before him. This is supported by the fact that it is mentioned after the story of Nuh and the rising of the water, because his saying "man qablahu" already includes them, so it is fitting to refer to their affair afterwards without explicit mention. Abu 'Amr, al-Kisa'i, 'Asim (in the narration of Aban), al-Hasan (in one of the reports from him), Abu Raja', al-Jahdari, and Talha read: "wa-man qibalahu" (وَمَن قِبَلَهُ), with a kasra on the qaf and a fatha on the ba', meaning his armies and the people of his obedience. This is supported by the fact that in the Mushaf of Ubayy ibn Ka'b it reads: [wa-ja'a Fir'awnu wa-man ma'ahu] (And Pharaoh came, and those with him), and in the codex of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari it reads: "wa-man tilqa'ahu" (وَمَن تِلْقاءَهُ) (those in front of him). Talha ibn Musarrif read: "wa-man hawlahu" (وَمَن حَوْلَهُ) (those around him).

"Qibal al-insan" (قِبَلُ الإنسانِ) means what is near him in place, and its usage became so common that it came to have the sense of: 'indi (عِنْدِي, with me), fi dhimmati (فِي ذِمَّتِي, in my responsibility), and ma yalini (ما يَلِينِي, what is close to me), in whatever way and whatever its sense.

"Al-Mu'tafikat" (الْمُؤْتَفِكاتُ): the towns of the people of Lut, peace be upon him. They were four, according to what has been narrated. "I'tafaka" means it was overturned, so that its upper part became its lower part. Thus "i'tafakat" (ائْتَفَكَتْ) means it was overturned, and it is "mu'tafika" (مُؤْتَفِكَةٌ). Al-Hasan read here: "wal-mu'tafikati" (والمُؤْتَفِكَةِ) in the singular. "Al-khati'a" (الخاطِئَةِ) is either an adjective of an omitted noun, as if he said: "bi-al-fi'li al-khati'a" (with the sinful act), or it intends the verbal noun, meaning with error in their disbelief and their disobedience.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So they disobeyed the messenger of their Lord﴾ may mean that "al-rasul" (الرَّسُولُ) is a generic noun, as if He said: those peoples and groups disobeyed the prophets of God, exalted is He, whom He sent to them. It may also mean that "al-rasul" has the sense of "al-risala" (the message). Al-Kalbi said: it refers to Musa, peace be upon him. Another, in the book of al-Tha'labi, said: it refers to Lut, peace be upon him. "Al-rabiya" (الرّابِيَةُ) is that which grows and has become very large, and from this comes "al-riba" (الرِّبا, increase/usury) and "riba al-mal" (increase of wealth), and from it [the verse] "it stirs and swells" (اهْتَزَّتْ ورَبَتْ).

Then He enumerated to the people His blessing in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, when the water rose high﴾. The meaning is: the water rose high at the time of the Flood which was upon the people of Nuh, peace be upon him. "Al-tughyan" (الطُّغْيانُ) is excess beyond the known limits of things. Its meaning is: it rose over its keepers in its outpouring, and over mankind in drowning them. Qatada said: it rose above everything by fifteen cubits. "Al-jariya" (الجارِيَةُ) is the ship.

The pronoun in His saying ﴿li-naj'alaha﴾ (that We might make it) refers to the act, meaning: whoever remembers it is restrained. It may also refer to "al-jariya", meaning: whoever hears of it takes heed. "Al-jariya" here is intended to mean the ship of Nuh, peace be upon him, as Mundhir said. Al-Mahdawi said: the meaning is: in the sailing ships. Qatada said: God preserved that ship until some of its planks were seen by the first of this Community and others, while the ships that were built after it had become ashes.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and an attentive ear might retain it﴾ is an expression for the understanding man, whose heart is illuminated, who hears speech and receives it with understanding and reflection. Abu 'Imran al-Jawni said: "wa'iya" (واعِيَةٌ) means it comprehended from God, mighty and majestic is He. It is narrated that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him: "I have asked God to make it your ear, O 'Ali." 'Ali, may God be pleased with him, said: "After that I did not hear anything and forget it."

Al-Jumhur read: "ta'iha" (تَعِيها) with a kasra on the 'ayn, on the pattern of "taliha" (تَلِيها). Ibn Kathir, in the narration of al-Hulwani, Qunbul, and Ibn Musarrif read: "wa-ta'iha" (وَتَعِيها) with a sukun on the 'ayn. They treated the ta' which is the sign of the present tense as equivalent to the kaf in "katif" (كَتِفٍ, shoulder), since the letter of the present tense is never separated from the verb, so it becomes quiescent for lightness, as one says "katf" (كَتْفٌ). A similar example is the saying of the poet:

Sulayma said: buy us some sawiq (a kind of food).

However, this line is detached (the sukun is not part of the same pattern as in the verse), so it is more remote, but the necessity of poetry permits it.

Then He mentioned the matter of the Resurrection. "Al-Sur" (الصُّورُ) is the horn into which it is blown. Sulayman ibn Arqam said: It reached me that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was asked about the Horn, and he said: "It is a horn of light, whose width is greater than the heavens." The blast referred to in this verse is the blast of the Resurrection that brings terror, and with it there will be swooning, then the blast of Resurrection. It was said: there are three blasts: the blast of terror, the blast of swooning, then the blast of resurrection. The reference in "this Our verse" is to the blast of terror, because the lifting of the mountains is its consequence. Al-Jumhur read: "nafkhatun" (نَفْخَةٌ) with a raf' (nominative), and since it is qualified, the raf' is correct. Abu al-Sammal read it in the accusative.

Most of the readers read: "wa-hamalat" (وَحَمَلَتْ) with a light mim, meaning: the winds and power have carried them. Ibn 'Amir, as is narrated from him, read: "wa-hammalat" (وَحَمَّلَتْ) with a doubled mim, and this has two possible meanings: one of them is that it is the carrier, which was carried by the power of God, mighty and majestic is He, and by violence and force that will pulverize them, so it is "muhammala" and "hamila" (carried and carrying). The other is that they are the carried, carried by angels or by power.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿fa-dukkata dakkatan wahida﴾ (then they were crushed with one crushing). He said "fa-dukkata" (فَدُكَّتا, the dual) although He had mentioned a plural, and this is acceptable because what was mentioned is two groups. This is like the saying of the poet:

Did it not grieve you that the ropes of my people and your people have been severed in separation?

From it is His saying: "kanata ratqan" (كانَتا رَتْقًا, were joined together). "Dukkata" (دُكَّتا) means: both of them were made level with the ground, as one says "naqa'a dakka'" (ناقَةٌ دَكّاءُ, a she-camel whose hump is flat), when she is weakened and her hump becomes level with her back.

"Al-waqi'a" (الواقِعَةُ) is the Resurrection, the greatest catastrophe. Some people said: it refers to the rock of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), but this is weak. "Inshiqaq al-sama'" (انْشِقاقُ السَّماءِ) is its splitting and the separation of some of its parts from others, and that is the weakness that befalls it, as one says of crumbling, cracked walls: "wahiya" (واهِيَةٌ, frail). "Al-malak" (المَلَكُ) is a generic noun, by which the angels are meant. Most of the exegetes said: the pronoun in "arja'iha" (أرْجائِها) refers to the sky, meaning the angels on its sides and what surrounds it. "Al-raja'" (الرَّجا) is the side of a wall, a well, or the like, and from it is the saying of the poet:

As if you had not seen before me a captive who was bound, nor a man thrown into al-Rajawan (a well).

That is: he is cast into a well and finds nothing to hold onto. Al-Dahhak also said, and Ibn Jubayr: the pronoun in "arja'iha" refers to the earth, even though it has not been mentioned nearby, because the context and the wording require that this be understood. He explained this verse by what is narrated: God, exalted is He, commands the angels of the lowest heaven, and they stand in rows on the edges of the earth. Then He commands the angels of the second heaven, and they line up behind them. Then likewise the angels of each heaven. So whenever any one of the jinn or humankind appears, he finds the earth encircled. They said: this is the explanation of this verse, and it is also the meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And your Lord comes, and the angels, row upon row﴾ (al-Fajr 22). It is also the explanation of His saying: "the Day of Calling, the Day you turn away retreating" according to the reading of the one who doubled the dal. And it is the explanation of His saying: ﴿O assembly of jinn and humankind, if you are able to pass through the regions of the heavens and the earth, then pass through; you will not pass except with authority﴾ (al-Rahman 33).

People differed concerning the eight who bear the Throne. Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with both of them, said: they are eight rows of angels, whose number no one knows. Ibn Zayd said: they are eight angels in the form of wild goats. A group of exegetes said: they are in the form of men, their feet beneath the lowest earth, and their heads and shoulders above the sky. It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "They are four today, and when the Day of Resurrection comes, God will strengthen them with four others besides them." The pronoun in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿above them﴾ is said to refer to the bearing angels, and it is said to refer to the whole world. Every power, however it is conceived, is only by the power and might of God.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 69, verses 9–17:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿And Pharaoh came, and those before him, and the overturned cities with sin.﴾ ﴿So they disobeyed the messenger of their Lord, and He seized them with a severe seizing.﴾ ﴿Indeed, when the water rose high, We carried you in the sailing ship.﴾ ﴿That We might make it for you a reminder, and that an attentive ear might retain it.﴾ ﴿Then when the Horn is blown with one blast.﴾ ﴿And the earth and the mountains are lifted and crushed with one crushing.﴾ ﴿So on that Day the Inevitable Event will occur.﴾ ﴿And the sky will split open, for it will be frail that Day.﴾ ﴿And the angels will be on its edges, and eight will bear above them, that Day, the Throne of your Lord.﴾

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Hamza, Abu Ja'far, Shayba, Abu 'Abd al-Rahman, and al-A'mash read: "wa-man qablahu" (وَمَن قَبْلَهُ) with a fatha on the qaf and a sukun on the ba', meaning the disbelieving nations who were before him. This is supported by the fact that it is mentioned after the story of Nuh and the rising of the water, because his saying "man qablahu" already includes them, so it is fitting to refer to their affair afterwards without explicit mention. Abu 'Amr, al-Kisa'i, 'Asim (in the narration of Aban), al-Hasan (in one of the reports from him), Abu Raja', al-Jahdari, and Talha read: "wa-man qibalahu" (وَمَن قِبَلَهُ), with a kasra on the qaf and a fatha on the ba', meaning his armies and the people of his obedience. This is supported by the fact that in the Mushaf of Ubayy ibn Ka'b it reads: [wa-ja'a Fir'awnu wa-man ma'ahu] (And Pharaoh came, and those with him), and in the codex of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari it reads: "wa-man tilqa'ahu" (وَمَن تِلْقاءَهُ) (those in front of him). Talha ibn Musarrif read: "wa-man hawlahu" (وَمَن حَوْلَهُ) (those around him).

"Qibal al-insan" (قِبَلُ الإنسانِ) means what is near him in place, and its usage became so common that it came to have the sense of: 'indi (عِنْدِي, with me), fi dhimmati (فِي ذِمَّتِي, in my responsibility), and ma yalini (ما يَلِينِي, what is close to me), in whatever way and whatever its sense.

"Al-Mu'tafikat" (الْمُؤْتَفِكاتُ): the towns of the people of Lut, peace be upon him. They were four, according to what has been narrated. "I'tafaka" means it was overturned, so that its upper part became its lower part. Thus "i'tafakat" (ائْتَفَكَتْ) means it was overturned, and it is "mu'tafika" (مُؤْتَفِكَةٌ). Al-Hasan read here: "wal-mu'tafikati" (والمُؤْتَفِكَةِ) in the singular. "Al-khati'a" (الخاطِئَةِ) is either an adjective of an omitted noun, as if he said: "bi-al-fi'li al-khati'a" (with the sinful act), or it intends the verbal noun, meaning with error in their disbelief and their disobedience.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So they disobeyed the messenger of their Lord﴾ may mean that "al-rasul" (الرَّسُولُ) is a generic noun, as if He said: those peoples and groups disobeyed the prophets of God, exalted is He, whom He sent to them. It may also mean that "al-rasul" has the sense of "al-risala" (the message). Al-Kalbi said: it refers to Musa, peace be upon him. Another, in the book of al-Tha'labi, said: it refers to Lut, peace be upon him. "Al-rabiya" (الرّابِيَةُ) is that which grows and has become very large, and from this comes "al-riba" (الرِّبا, increase/usury) and "riba al-mal" (increase of wealth), and from it [the verse] "it stirs and swells" (اهْتَزَّتْ ورَبَتْ).

Then He enumerated to the people His blessing in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, when the water rose high﴾. The meaning is: the water rose high at the time of the Flood which was upon the people of Nuh, peace be upon him. "Al-tughyan" (الطُّغْيانُ) is excess beyond the known limits of things. Its meaning is: it rose over its keepers in its outpouring, and over mankind in drowning them. Qatada said: it rose above everything by fifteen cubits. "Al-jariya" (الجارِيَةُ) is the ship.

The pronoun in His saying ﴿li-naj'alaha﴾ (that We might make it) refers to the act, meaning: whoever remembers it is restrained. It may also refer to "al-jariya", meaning: whoever hears of it takes heed. "Al-jariya" here is intended to mean the ship of Nuh, peace be upon him, as Mundhir said. Al-Mahdawi said: the meaning is: in the sailing ships. Qatada said: God preserved that ship until some of its planks were seen by the first of this Community and others, while the ships that were built after it had become ashes.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and an attentive ear might retain it﴾ is an expression for the understanding man, whose heart is illuminated, who hears speech and receives it with understanding and reflection. Abu 'Imran al-Jawni said: "wa'iya" (واعِيَةٌ) means it comprehended from God, mighty and majestic is He. It is narrated that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him: "I have asked God to make it your ear, O 'Ali." 'Ali, may God be pleased with him, said: "After that I did not hear anything and forget it."

Al-Jumhur read: "ta'iha" (تَعِيها) with a kasra on the 'ayn, on the pattern of "taliha" (تَلِيها). Ibn Kathir, in the narration of al-Hulwani, Qunbul, and Ibn Musarrif read: "wa-ta'iha" (وَتَعِيها) with a sukun on the 'ayn. They treated the ta' which is the sign of the present tense as equivalent to the kaf in "katif" (كَتِفٍ, shoulder), since the letter of the present tense is never separated from the verb, so it becomes quiescent for lightness, as one says "katf" (كَتْفٌ). A similar example is the saying of the poet:

Sulayma said: buy us some sawiq (a kind of food).

However, this line is detached (the sukun is not part of the same pattern as in the verse), so it is more remote, but the necessity of poetry permits it.

Then He mentioned the matter of the Resurrection. "Al-Sur" (الصُّورُ) is the horn into which it is blown. Sulayman ibn Arqam said: It reached me that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was asked about the Horn, and he said: "It is a horn of light, whose width is greater than the heavens." The blast referred to in this verse is the blast of the Resurrection that brings terror, and with it there will be swooning, then the blast of Resurrection. It was said: there are three blasts: the blast of terror, the blast of swooning, then the blast of resurrection. The reference in "this Our verse" is to the blast of terror, because the lifting of the mountains is its consequence. Al-Jumhur read: "nafkhatun" (نَفْخَةٌ) with a raf' (nominative), and since it is qualified, the raf' is correct. Abu al-Sammal read it in the accusative.

Most of the readers read: "wa-hamalat" (وَحَمَلَتْ) with a light mim, meaning: the winds and power have carried them. Ibn 'Amir, as is narrated from him, read: "wa-hammalat" (وَحَمَّلَتْ) with a doubled mim, and this has two possible meanings: one of them is that it is the carrier, which was carried by the power of God, mighty and majestic is He, and by violence and force that will pulverize them, so it is "muhammala" and "hamila" (carried and carrying). The other is that they are the carried, carried by angels or by power.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿fa-dukkata dakkatan wahida﴾ (then they were crushed with one crushing). He said "fa-dukkata" (فَدُكَّتا, the dual) although He had mentioned a plural, and this is acceptable because what was mentioned is two groups. This is like the saying of the poet:

Did it not grieve you that the ropes of my people and your people have been severed in separation?

From it is His saying: "kanata ratqan" (كانَتا رَتْقًا, were joined together). "Dukkata" (دُكَّتا) means: both of them were made level with the ground, as one says "naqa'a dakka'" (ناقَةٌ دَكّاءُ, a she-camel whose hump is flat), when she is weakened and her hump becomes level with her back.

"Al-waqi'a" (الواقِعَةُ) is the Resurrection, the greatest catastrophe. Some people said: it refers to the rock of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), but this is weak. "Inshiqaq al-sama'" (انْشِقاقُ السَّماءِ) is its splitting and the separation of some of its parts from others, and that is the weakness that befalls it, as one says of crumbling, cracked walls: "wahiya" (واهِيَةٌ, frail). "Al-malak" (المَلَكُ) is a generic noun, by which the angels are meant. Most of the exegetes said: the pronoun in "arja'iha" (أرْجائِها) refers to the sky, meaning the angels on its sides and what surrounds it. "Al-raja'" (الرَّجا) is the side of a wall, a well, or the like, and from it is the saying of the poet:

As if you had not seen before me a captive who was bound, nor a man thrown into al-Rajawan (a well).

That is: he is cast into a well and finds nothing to hold onto. Al-Dahhak also said, and Ibn Jubayr: the pronoun in "arja'iha" refers to the earth, even though it has not been mentioned nearby, because the context and the wording require that this be understood. He explained this verse by what is narrated: God, exalted is He, commands the angels of the lowest heaven, and they stand in rows on the edges of the earth. Then He commands the angels of the second heaven, and they line up behind them. Then likewise the angels of each heaven. So whenever any one of the jinn or humankind appears, he finds the earth encircled. They said: this is the explanation of this verse, and it is also the meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And your Lord comes, and the angels, row upon row﴾ (al-Fajr 22). It is also the explanation of His saying: "the Day of Calling, the Day you turn away retreating" according to the reading of the one who doubled the dal. And it is the explanation of His saying: ﴿O assembly of jinn and humankind, if you are able to pass through the regions of the heavens and the earth, then pass through; you will not pass except with authority﴾ (al-Rahman 33).

People differed concerning the eight who bear the Throne. Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with both of them, said: they are eight rows of angels, whose number no one knows. Ibn Zayd said: they are eight angels in the form of wild goats. A group of exegetes said: they are in the form of men, their feet beneath the lowest earth, and their heads and shoulders above the sky. It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "They are four today, and when the Day of Resurrection comes, God will strengthen them with four others besides them." The pronoun in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿above them﴾ is said to refer to the bearing angels, and it is said to refer to the whole world. Every power, however it is conceived, is only by the power and might of God.

He explained this verse by what is narrated: God, exalted is He, commands the angels of the lowest heaven, and they stand in rows on the edges of the earth. Then He commands the angels of the second heaven, and they line up behind them. Then likewise the angels of each heaven. Ibn Zayd said: they are eight angels in the form of wild goats. A group of exegetes said: they are in the form of men, their feet beneath the lowest earth, and their heads and shoulders above the sky. [p. 392] His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

The address in His saying ﴿you will be exposed﴾ is to all of the created beings. It is narrated from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari and Ibn Mas'ud that on the Day of Resurrection there are two exposures (ʿurḍatān), in which there are excuses, questioning, disputes and argument. The rest of the readers read it with the letter ta (la takhfā), in consideration of the feminine form of ﴿خافِيَةٌ﴾ (khafiyah, "hidden thing"), and this is the reading of the majority (al-Jumhur). His saying ﴿خافِيَةٌ﴾ means: a secret thought or a hidden belief.

﴿Those who are given their books in their right hands﴾ are those who will abide forever in the Garden, the people of faith. The people of knowledge and reason have differed concerning the group among the people of sins upon whom the threat is carried out: when do they receive their books? Some of them said: the more evident view is that they receive them along with the people, and this comforts them during the period of punishment. Al-Hasan said: when one is given his book in his right hand, he will not read it until Allah permits him; then, when He permits him, he will say: ﴿"Here, read my record!"﴾. Others said: the more evident view is that when they are brought out of the Fire, faith comforts them at the time of punishment.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is the apparent meaning of this verse, because how could one who is heading to the Fire say ﴿"Here, read my record!"﴾?

As for the word ﴿هاؤُمُ﴾ (hā'um, "here"), some people said its original form is ﴿هاؤُمُوا﴾ (hā'umū), then it was shortened by lightening and common usage. Others said that this ﴿مِيمُ﴾ (mīm) is the pronoun of the plural. There is an examination of all of this, but the meaning in every case is: "Come!" It is a summons to the act that is commanded. His saying ﴿اقْرَءُوا كِتابِيَهْ﴾ ("read my record") expresses joy and delight.

His saying ﴿إنِّي ظَنَنْتُ﴾ (innī ẓanantu, "indeed I was certain") — the verse is an expression of his faith in the Resurrection and other matters. Qatadah said: he held this as a certain conviction (ẓann yaqīn), so it benefited him; and some people held it as a doubtful suspicion (ẓann shakk), so they were wretched by it. The word ﴿ظَنَنْتُ﴾ here stands in the place of ﴿تَيَقَّنْتُ﴾ (tayaqqantu, "I was certain"), and it concerns something certain that has not yet happened nor come into the realm of the senses. This is the category of ẓann that takes the place of yaqīn (certainty). [p. 393]

Some readers read ﴿كِتابِيَهْ﴾, ﴿حِسابِيَهْ﴾, ﴿مالِيَهْ﴾ and ﴿سُلْطانِيَهْ﴾ with the letter hā' (ha, the final "h" sound) both when continuing and when pausing, following the script of the Mushaf. In continuing speech it is with the intention of pausing, because it is the hā' al-sakt (the silent pausal hā'), so it has no meaning in continuous speech. Al-A'mash and Ibn Abi Ishaq dropped the hā's in continuous speech but not in pause. Abu Hatim said: our reading is to affirm the hā's in pause and drop them in continuous speech, and Ibn Abi Muhaysin and Salam read in this way. Al-Zahrawi said: affirming the hā' in continuous speech is a grammatical error (lahn) that no one I know of permits.

﴿Quṭūf﴾ (القُطُوفُ, "fruits") is the plural of qaṭf, which is what is picked from fruit trees and plucked. Its being ﴿دانِيَةٌ﴾ (dāniyah, "within reach") means that they come to hand as one wishes; so the one standing, the one sitting and the one lying down eat from them, with their mouths, from its tree. ﴿Aslaftum﴾ (أسْلَفْتُمْ, "you advanced") means: you sent ahead. ﴿Al-Ayyām al-Khāliyah﴾ (الأيّامُ الخالِيَةُ, "the days gone by") are the days of this world, because in the Hereafter they have passed and gone. **Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 69, verses 18–29:**

[p. 392] His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿On that Day you will be exposed; not a thing of yours will be hidden.﴾ ﴿As for him who is given his record in his right hand, he will say: "Here, read my record!"﴾ ﴿"Indeed, I was certain that I would meet my reckoning."﴾ ﴿So he will be in a pleasing life﴾ ﴿in an elevated Garden,﴾ ﴿its fruits within reach.﴾ ﴿"Eat and drink with satisfaction for what you advanced in the days gone by."﴾ ﴿But as for him who is given his record in his left hand, he will say: "Oh, I wish I had not been given my record,﴾ ﴿and had not known my reckoning!﴾ ﴿Oh, I wish it had been the decisive end!﴾ ﴿My wealth has not availed me;﴾ ﴿my authority has gone from me."﴾

The address in His saying ﴿you will be exposed﴾ is to all of the created beings. It is narrated from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari and Ibn Mas'ud that on the Day of Resurrection there are two exposures (ʿurḍatān), in which there are excuses, questioning, disputes and argument. Then there will be a third exposure, in which the pages will fly about, some into right hands and some into left hands.

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read ﴿لا يَخْفى﴾ (la yakhfā, with the letter ya), and this is the reading of Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, Ibn Wathhab, Talhah, al-A'mash and Isa. The rest of the readers read it with the letter ta (la takhfā), in consideration of the feminine form of ﴿خافِيَةٌ﴾ (khafiyah, "hidden thing"), and this is the reading of the majority (al-Jumhur). His saying ﴿خافِيَةٌ﴾ means: a secret thought or a hidden belief.

﴿Those who are given their books in their right hands﴾ are those who will abide forever in the Garden, the people of faith. The people of knowledge and reason have differed concerning the group among the people of sins upon whom the threat is carried out: when do they receive their books? Some of them said: the more evident view is that they receive them along with the people, and this comforts them during the period of punishment. Al-Hasan said: when one is given his book in his right hand, he will not read it until Allah permits him; then, when He permits him, he will say: ﴿"Here, read my record!"﴾. Others said: the more evident view is that when they are brought out of the Fire, faith comforts them at the time of punishment.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is the apparent meaning of this verse, because how could one who is heading to the Fire say ﴿"Here, read my record!"﴾?

As for the word ﴿هاؤُمُ﴾ (hā'um, "here"), some people said its original form is ﴿هاؤُمُوا﴾ (hā'umū), then it was shortened by lightening and common usage. Others said that this ﴿مِيمُ﴾ (mīm) is the pronoun of the plural. There is an examination of all of this, but the meaning in every case is: "Come!" It is a summons to the act that is commanded. His saying ﴿اقْرَءُوا كِتابِيَهْ﴾ ("read my record") expresses joy and delight.

His saying ﴿إنِّي ظَنَنْتُ﴾ (innī ẓanantu, "indeed I was certain") — the verse is an expression of his faith in the Resurrection and other matters. Qatadah said: he held this as a certain conviction (ẓann yaqīn), so it benefited him; and some people held it as a doubtful suspicion (ẓann shakk), so they were wretched by it. The word ﴿ظَنَنْتُ﴾ here stands in the place of ﴿تَيَقَّنْتُ﴾ (tayaqqantu, "I was certain"), and it concerns something certain that has not yet happened nor come into the realm of the senses. This is the category of ẓann that takes the place of yaqīn (certainty). [p. 393]

Some readers read ﴿كِتابِيَهْ﴾, ﴿حِسابِيَهْ﴾, ﴿مالِيَهْ﴾ and ﴿سُلْطانِيَهْ﴾ with the letter hā' (ha, the final "h" sound) both when continuing and when pausing, following the script of the Mushaf. In continuing speech it is with the intention of pausing, because it is the hā' al-sakt (the silent pausal hā'), so it has no meaning in continuous speech. Al-A'mash and Ibn Abi Ishaq dropped the hā's in continuous speech but not in pause. Abu Hatim said: our reading is to affirm the hā's in pause and drop them in continuous speech, and Ibn Abi Muhaysin and Salam read in this way. Al-Zahrawi said: affirming the hā' in continuous speech is a grammatical error (lahn) that no one I know of permits.

﴿Raḍiyah﴾ (راضِيَةٍ, "pleasing") means: possessing satisfaction (dhāt riḍan), so it has the meaning of marḍiyyah (pleasing/approved), and it is not the form of an active participle (ism fā'il). ﴿ʿĀliyah﴾ (عالِيَةٍ, "elevated") means: in place, in rank, and in all aspects of loftiness.

﴿Quṭūf﴾ (القُطُوفُ, "fruits") is the plural of qaṭf, which is what is picked from fruit trees and plucked. Its being ﴿دانِيَةٌ﴾ (dāniyah, "within reach") means that they come to hand as one wishes; so the one standing, the one sitting and the one lying down eat from them, with their mouths, from its tree. ﴿Aslaftum﴾ (أسْلَفْتُمْ, "you advanced") means: you sent ahead. ﴿Al-Ayyām al-Khāliyah﴾ (الأيّامُ الخالِيَةُ, "the days gone by") are the days of this world, because in the Hereafter they have passed and gone. Waki', Ibn Jubayr and Abd al-Aziz ibn Rafi' said: what is meant by ﴿what you advanced﴾ is fasting. Yet its generality over all deeds is more preferable and better.

﴿Those who are given their books in their left hands﴾ are those who will abide forever in the Fire, the people of disbelief. They will wish that they had been non-existent, so that nothing would befall them. His saying ﴿"Oh, I wish it had been the decisive end!"﴾ is an allusion to the death of this world, meaning: "I wish there were no return after it, nor any life." Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 69, verses 30–40:

(p-394) The Exalted and Majestic One said:

﴿Seize him and shackle him,﴾ ﴿then burn him in the Blazing Fire.﴾ ﴿Then insert him into a chain whose length is seventy cubits; so thread him.﴾ ﴿Indeed, he did not believe in Allah, the Mighty,﴾ ﴿and did not urge the feeding of the needy.﴾ ﴿So today he has no close friend here,﴾ ﴿nor any food except from ghislin,﴾ ﴿which none eat except the sinners.﴾ ﴿So I swear by what you see,﴾ ﴿and what you do not see,﴾ ﴿that this is indeed the word of a noble Messenger.﴾

The meaning: Allah the Exalted says, or the angel by His command says, to the guards (al-zabaniyya): "Seize him and shackle him," i.e., place a shackle upon his neck. Ibn Jarir said: it was revealed concerning Abu Jahl.

And "dhar'uha" means the measure of its length. Allah the Exalted has made seventy, seven hundred, and seven as stopping points and limits for great things, and this is the custom of the Arabs and others in treating them as limits. This chain is among the things in which Allah the Exalted made seventy the limit. Al-Suddi recited "dhar'uha sab'īn" with a yā', and this is by omitting the predicate of the subject (ḥadhf khabar al-ibtidā'). People differed about the measure of this cubit. Ibn 'Abbas, Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir, and Ibn Jurayj said: it is the cubit of the king. Nawf al-Bakali and others said: in the cubit are seventy spans (bā'), in each span as much as the distance between Kufa and Makka. This requires a chain of transmission. Some skilled exegetes said: it is the cubit well known to us, and we were addressed with what we know and can grasp. Al-Hasan said: Allah knows best which cubit it is. Suwayd ibn Najih said, in the book of al-Tha'labi: "It has reached me that all the people of the Fire are in that chain." Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: "If a link of it were placed upon a mountain, it would melt like lead."

His saying, "fa-uslukūhu" means: enter him (fa-dkhulūhu). From it is the words of Abu Wajza al-Sa'di describing wild asses:

؎ Until they threaded the hides of them into a musk of the offspring of the wide-ranging, fine-skinned mother...

(p-395) It is reported that this chain enters the mouth of the disbeliever and comes out from his rear. Thus, in reality, it is what is threaded into him, but the speech follows the pattern of their saying: "I put the cap on my head," and "my mouth in the stone." It is also reported that this chain is wound around the disbeliever until it suffocates him and squeezes him. Thus the speech, on this view, is in its literal sense, and he is the one threaded.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and did not urge the feeding of the needy﴾ — what is meant is: urging the giving of food to the needy. The attribution of the food to the needy is because the needy has some connection to it. This quality was singled out among the disbeliever's traits for mention because it is among the most harmful of traits among humans; when it spreads among a people, their needy perish.

The commentators differed concerning His saying, "ḥamīm." Most exegetes said: it is the close friend of tender affection. Thus Allah the Exalted negated that the disbeliever would have anyone there who would befriend him, and negated that he would have any food except from ghislin. Muhammad ibn al-Mustanir said: al-ḥamīm is hot water. So it is as if He, the Exalted, informed that the disbeliever has no water, nor any liquid, nor any food except from ghislin. The linguists said that it is what flows from wounds when they are washed. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is the pus of the people of the Fire. Qatada and Ibn Zayd said: ghislin and zaqqum are the most wicked and most repulsive of things. al-Dahhak and al-Rabi' said: it is a tree that the people of the Fire eat. Some exegetes said: it is something that flows from ḍarī' (a thorny plant), because Allah the Exalted has informed that for them there is no food except from ḍarī', and in another verse, except from ghislin; so they are one thing, or two interlocking things. It is possible that the information here concerns one group and there concerns another, and that ghislin and ḍarī' are distinct, as is understood in the Arabic language. The predicate of "laysa" is "lahu," and al-Mahdawi said: it is not correct for "hāhunā" to be the predicate.

The qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

And that may be correct, Allah willing.

(p-396) The "khāti'" is one who does the opposite of what is right deliberately, while the "mukhti'" is one who does it without intent. Al-Hasan and al-Zuhri recited "al-khāṭiyūn" with a yā' without hamza; Ṭalḥa, Abu Ja'far, Shayba, and Nafi' (with a variant from him) recited "al-khāṭṭūn" with a ḍamma on the ṭā' without hamza.

His saying, the Exalted: "fa-lā uqsimu" — some grammarians said "lā" is superfluous, and the meaning is "fa-aqsama." Others among them said: "lā" is a refutation of what preceded of the disbelievers' statements, and the beginning is "uqsimu." Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan recited "fa-la'uqsimu," because the lām of the oath accompanies the alif of "uqsimu."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿by what you see﴾ ﴿and what you do not see﴾ — Qatada ibn di'ama said: Allah intended to generalize the oath to all His creation. Others said: it means bodies and spirits.

The qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is a good, general view. And it was said: a good, general view.

Ibn 'Ata' said: what you see of the traces of power and what you do not see of the traces of power. Some people said: by His saying, glorified and exalted, "and what you do not see," He meant the angels.

"The noble Messenger" is, according to a group of scholars, Gabriel, peace be upon him, and according to others, Muhammad ﷺ. The speech is attributed to him because he is the one who conveyed it and delivered it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 69, verses 41–52:

His Exalted and Majestic saying:

﴿And it is not the word of a poet; little is it that you believe﴾ ﴿Nor the word of a soothsayer; little is it that you remember﴾ ﴿A revelation from the Lord of the worlds﴾ ﴿And if he had fabricated against Us some sayings﴾ ﴿We would have seized him by the right hand﴾ ﴿Then We would have cut from him the aorta﴾ ﴿And none of you could have prevented Us from him﴾ ﴿And indeed, it is a reminder for the God-fearing﴾ ﴿And indeed, We know that among you are deniers﴾ ﴿And indeed, it is a regret for the disbelievers﴾ ﴿And indeed, it is the certain truth﴾ ﴿So glorify the name of your Lord, the Mighty﴾

The Exalted negated that the Qur'an is the word of a poet, as Quraysh claimed. "Qalīlan" (little) is in the accusative by a hidden verb indicated by "tu'minūn" (you believe). The "mā" may be a negative particle, in which case their belief is entirely negated; or it may be a verbal-masdar particle (mā maṣdariyya), in which case what is described as little is either the belief itself or the number of those who believe. If their belief is described as little, then it is linguistic belief (al-īmān al-lughawī), because they affirmed a few matters that do not avail them anything, since they used to affirm that goodness, kinship ties, and chastity, which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded, were correct. Then the Exalted negated that the "Qur'an" is the word of a soothsayer, as some of them claimed. Ibn Kathīr, Ibn ʿĀmir, al-Ḥasan, and al-Jaḥdarī read "qalīlan mā yu'minūn" and "qalīlan mā yadhdhakkarūn" with the ya' in both; the rest read them with the tā' from above. Abū ʿAmr preferred the reading with the tā' from above based on His saying "fa-mā minkum" (so none of you). In the Muṣḥaf of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb it is "mā tatadhakkarūn" with two tā's. "Tanzīl" (revelation) is in the nominative as a subject, meaning: it is a revelation. Then the Exalted informed that if Muḥammad had fabricated something against Us, He would punish him with what was mentioned. Taqawwul is when a person attributes to another that he said something he did not say. Dhakwān and his son Muḥammad read "wa-law yaqūlu ʿalaynā" with the ya' and a damma on the qāf; this reading is an allusion (taʿrīḍ) to what the reading of the majority states explicitly, and the allusion is clarified by His saying "ʿalaynā baʿḍa al-aqāwīl" (some sayings against Us).

As for His saying "La-akhadhnā minhu bil-yamīn" (We would have seized him by the right hand), its meaning has been disputed. Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "bil-yamīn" means "with power," and the meaning is: We would have reached His punishment with power from Us; or the meaning is: We would have taken away his strength. Others said it is an expression for humiliation, as one says of someone who is imprisoned or set up for punishment: "He has taken him by the hand and by the right hand."

"Al-Waṭīn" is the sinews of the heart (niyāṭ al-qalb), as Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, said. It is a thick vein that the blade of the slaughterer meets. From it is the saying of al-Shammākh:

"When you carry me and load my saddle to ʿArāba, then choke with the blood of the waṭīn."

So the meaning of the verse: We would have hastened to take away his life. "Al-ḥājiz" is the preventer, and the plural "ḥājizīn" is in consideration of the meaning of "aḥad" (anyone), since it applies to the plural; similar to His peace and blessings be upon him saying: "Spoils were not made lawful for anyone before you except the heads (ruʾūs)."

The pronoun in His saying "wa-innahu la-tadhkiratun" (and indeed, it is a reminder) refers to the Qur'an, and it was said that it refers to Muḥammad (ﷺ). His saying "wa-innā la-naʿlamu anna minkum mukadhdhibīn" (and indeed, We know that among you are deniers) is a warning (waʿīd). Its being a regret for the disbelievers is from the standpoint that they disbelieved, and they see that whoever believed in it is blessed while they are punished.

As for His saying "wa-innahu la-ḥaqqu al-yaqīn" (and indeed, it is the certain truth), the Kufans held that it is an idāfa of a thing to itself, like "dār al-ākhira" and "masjid al-jāmiʿ." The Basrans and the skilled grammarians held that "ḥaqq" is idāfa to the most eloquent of its aspects. Al-Mubarrad said: it is only like your saying "ʿayn al-yaqīn" and "maḥḍ al-yaqīn."

Then Allah the Exalted commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to glorify the name of his great Lord, and within that is persistence in his message, proceeding to perform and convey it. It is narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said when this verse was revealed: "Make it in your ruku'." A group of scholars recommended adhering to this, while Mālik disliked making it obligatory, lest it be regarded as an obligatory duty.

The commentary of Surah [al-Ḥāqqa] is complete, and praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds.

His Exalted and Majestic saying:

﴿And it is not the word of a poet; little is it that you believe﴾ ﴿Nor the word of a soothsayer; little is it that you remember﴾ ﴿A revelation from the Lord of the worlds﴾ ﴿And if he had fabricated against Us some sayings﴾ ﴿We would have seized him by the right hand﴾ ﴿Then We would have cut from him the aorta﴾ ﴿And none of you could have prevented Us from him﴾ ﴿And indeed, it is a reminder for the God-fearing﴾ ﴿And indeed, We know that among you are deniers﴾ ﴿And indeed, it is a regret for the disbelievers﴾ ﴿And indeed, it is the certain truth﴾ ﴿So glorify the name of your Lord, the Mighty﴾

The Exalted negated that the Qur'an is the word of a poet, as Quraysh claimed. "Qalīlan" (little) is in the accusative by a hidden verb indicated by "tu'minūn" (you believe). The "mā" may be a negative particle, in which case their belief is entirely negated; or it may be a verbal-masdar particle (mā maṣdariyya), in which case what is described as little is either the belief itself or the number of those who believe. If their belief is described as little, then it is linguistic belief (al-īmān al-lughawī), because they affirmed a few matters that do not avail them anything, since they used to affirm that goodness, kinship ties, and chastity, which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded, were correct. Then the Exalted negated that the "Qur'an" is the word of a soothsayer, as some of them claimed. Ibn Kathīr, Ibn ʿĀmir, al-Ḥasan, and al-Jaḥdarī read "qalīlan mā yu'minūn" and "qalīlan mā yadhdhakkarūn" with the ya' in both; the rest read them with the tā' from above. Abū ʿAmr preferred the reading with the tā' from above based on His saying "fa-mā minkum" (so none of you). In the Muṣḥaf of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb it is "mā tatadhakkarūn" with two tā's. "Tanzīl" (revelation) is in the nominative as a subject, meaning: it is a revelation. Then the Exalted informed that if Muḥammad had fabricated something against Us, He would punish him with what was mentioned. Taqawwul is when a person attributes to another that he said something he did not say. Dhakwān and his son Muḥammad read "wa-law yaqūlu ʿalaynā" with the ya' and a damma on the qāf; this reading is an allusion (taʿrīḍ) to what the reading of the majority states explicitly, and the allusion is clarified by His saying "ʿalaynā baʿḍa al-aqāwīl" (some sayings against Us).

As for His saying "La-akhadhnā minhu bil-yamīn" (We would have seized him by the right hand), its meaning has been disputed. Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "bil-yamīn" means "with power," and the meaning is: We would have reached His punishment with power from Us; or the meaning is: We would have taken away his strength. Others said it is an expression for humiliation, as one says of someone who is imprisoned or set up for punishment: "He has taken him by the hand and by the right hand."

"Al-Waṭīn" is the sinews of the heart (niyāṭ al-qalb), as Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, said. It is a thick vein that the blade of the slaughterer meets. From it is the saying of al-Shammākh:

"When you carry me and load my saddle to ʿArāba, then choke with the blood of the waṭīn."

So the meaning of the verse: We would have hastened to take away his life. "Al-ḥājiz" is the preventer, and the plural "ḥājizīn" is in consideration of the meaning of "aḥad" (anyone), since it applies to the plural; similar to His peace and blessings be upon him saying: "Spoils were not made lawful for anyone before you except the heads (ruʾūs)."

The pronoun in His saying "wa-innahu la-tadhkiratun" (and indeed, it is a reminder) refers to the Qur'an, and it was said that it refers to Muḥammad (ﷺ). His saying "wa-innā la-naʿlamu anna minkum mukadhdhibīn" (and indeed, We know that among you are deniers) is a warning (waʿīd). Its being a regret for the disbelievers is from the standpoint that they disbelieved, and they see that whoever believed in it is blessed while they are punished.

As for His saying "wa-innahu la-ḥaqqu al-yaqīn" (and indeed, it is the certain truth), the Kufans held that it is an idāfa of a thing to itself, like "dār al-ākhira" and "masjid al-jāmiʿ." The Basrans and the skilled grammarians held that "ḥaqq" is idāfa to the most eloquent of its aspects. Al-Mubarrad said: it is only like your saying "ʿayn al-yaqīn" and "maḥḍ al-yaqīn."

Then Allah the Exalted commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to glorify the name of his great Lord, and within that is persistence in his message, proceeding to perform and convey it. It is narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said when this verse was revealed: "Make it in your ruku'." A group of scholars recommended adhering to this, while Mālik disliked making it obligatory, lest it be regarded as an obligatory duty.

The commentary of Surah [al-Ḥāqqa] is complete, and praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds.

﴿And it is not the word of a poet; little is it that you believe﴾ ﴿Nor the word of a soothsayer; little is it that you remember﴾ ﴿A revelation from the Lord of the worlds﴾ ﴿And if he had fabricated against Us some sayings﴾ ﴿We would have seized him by the right hand﴾ ﴿Then We would have cut from him the aorta﴾ ﴿And none of you could have prevented Us from him﴾ ﴿And indeed, it is a reminder for the God-fearing﴾ ﴿And indeed, We know that among you are deniers﴾ ﴿And indeed, it is a regret for the disbelievers﴾ ﴿And indeed, it is the certain truth﴾ ﴿So glorify the name of your Lord, the Mighty﴾

The Exalted negated that the Qur'an is the word of a poet, as Quraysh claimed. "Qalīlan" (little) is in the accusative by a hidden verb indicated by "tu'minūn" (you believe). The "mā" may be a negative particle, in which case their belief is entirely negated; or it may be a verbal-masdar particle (mā maṣdariyya), in which case what is described as little is either the belief itself or the number of those who believe. If their belief is described as little, then it is linguistic belief (al-īmān al-lughawī), because they affirmed a few matters that do not avail them anything, since they used to affirm that goodness, kinship ties, and chastity, which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded, were correct. Then the Exalted negated that the "Qur'an" is the word of a soothsayer, as some of them claimed. Ibn Kathīr, Ibn ʿĀmir, al-Ḥasan, and al-Jaḥdarī read "qalīlan mā yu'minūn" and "qalīlan mā yadhdhakkarūn" with the ya' in both; the rest read them with the tā' from above. Abū ʿAmr preferred the reading with the tā' from above based on His saying "fa-mā minkum" (so none of you). In the Muṣḥaf of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb it is "mā tatadhakkarūn" with two tā's. "Tanzīl" (revelation) is in the nominative as a subject, meaning: it is a revelation. Then the Exalted informed that if Muḥammad had fabricated something against Us, He would punish him with what was mentioned. Taqawwul is when a person attributes to another that he said something he did not say. Dhakwān and his son Muḥammad read "wa-law yaqūlu ʿalaynā" with the ya' and a damma on the qāf; this reading is an allusion (taʿrīḍ) to what the reading of the majority states explicitly, and the allusion is clarified by His saying "ʿalaynā baʿḍa al-aqāwīl" (some sayings against Us).

As for His saying "La-akhadhnā minhu bil-yamīn" (We would have seized him by the right hand), its meaning has been disputed. Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "bil-yamīn" means "with power," and the meaning is: We would have reached His punishment with power from Us; or the meaning is: We would have taken away his strength. Others said it is an expression for humiliation, as one says of someone who is imprisoned or set up for punishment: "He has taken him by the hand and by the right hand."

"Al-Waṭīn" is the sinews of the heart (niyāṭ al-qalb), as Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, said. It is a thick vein that the blade of the slaughterer meets. From it is the saying of al-Shammākh:

"When you carry me and load my saddle to ʿArāba, then choke with the blood of the waṭīn."

So the meaning of the verse: We would have hastened to take away his life. "Al-ḥājiz" is the preventer, and the plural "ḥājizīn" is in consideration of the meaning of "aḥad" (anyone), since it applies to the plural; similar to His peace and blessings be upon him saying: "Spoils were not made lawful for anyone before you except the heads (ruʾūs)."

The pronoun in His saying "wa-innahu la-tadhkiratun" (and indeed, it is a reminder) refers to the Qur'an, and it was said that it refers to Muḥammad (ﷺ). His saying "wa-innā la-naʿlamu anna minkum mukadhdhibīn" (and indeed, We know that among you are deniers) is a warning (waʿīd). Its being a regret for the disbelievers is from the standpoint that they disbelieved, and they see that whoever believed in it is blessed while they are punished.

As for His saying "wa-innahu la-ḥaqqu al-yaqīn" (and indeed, it is the certain truth), the Kufans held that it is an idāfa of a thing to itself, like "dār al-ākhira" and "masjid al-jāmiʿ." The Basrans and the skilled grammarians held that "ḥaqq" is idāfa to the most eloquent of its aspects. Al-Mubarrad said: it is only like your saying "ʿayn al-yaqīn" and "maḥḍ al-yaqīn."

Then Allah the Exalted commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to glorify the name of his great Lord, and within that is persistence in his message, proceeding to perform and convey it. It is narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said when this verse was revealed: "Make it in your ruku'." A group of scholars recommended adhering to this, while Mālik disliked making it obligatory, lest it be regarded as an obligatory duty.

The commentary of Surah [al-Ḥāqqa] is complete, and praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 69, verses 41–52:

His Exalted and Majestic saying:

﴿And it is not the word of a poet; little is it that you believe﴾ ﴿Nor the word of a soothsayer; little is it that you remember﴾ ﴿A revelation from the Lord of the worlds﴾ ﴿And if he had fabricated against Us some sayings﴾ ﴿We would have seized him by the right hand﴾ ﴿Then We would have cut from him the aorta﴾ ﴿And none of you could have prevented Us from him﴾ ﴿And indeed, it is a reminder for the God-fearing﴾ ﴿And indeed, We know that among you are deniers﴾ ﴿And indeed, it is a regret for the disbelievers﴾ ﴿And indeed, it is the certain truth﴾ ﴿So glorify the name of your Lord, the Mighty﴾

The Exalted negated that the Qur'an is the word of a poet, as Quraysh claimed. "Qalīlan" (little) is in the accusative by a hidden verb indicated by "tu'minūn" (you believe). The "mā" may be a negative particle, in which case their belief is entirely negated; or it may be a verbal-masdar particle (mā maṣdariyya), in which case what is described as little is either the belief itself or the number of those who believe. If their belief is described as little, then it is linguistic belief (al-īmān al-lughawī), because they affirmed a few matters that do not avail them anything, since they used to affirm that goodness, kinship ties, and chastity, which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded, were correct. Then the Exalted negated that the "Qur'an" is the word of a soothsayer, as some of them claimed. Ibn Kathīr, Ibn ʿĀmir, al-Ḥasan, and al-Jaḥdarī read "qalīlan mā yu'minūn" and "qalīlan mā yadhdhakkarūn" with the ya' in both; the rest read them with the tā' from above. Abū ʿAmr preferred the reading with the tā' from above based on His saying "fa-mā minkum" (so none of you). In the Muṣḥaf of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb it is "mā tatadhakkarūn" with two tā's. "Tanzīl" (revelation) is in the nominative as a subject, meaning: it is a revelation. Then the Exalted informed that if Muḥammad had fabricated something against Us, He would punish him with what was mentioned. Taqawwul is when a person attributes to another that he said something he did not say. Dhakwān and his son Muḥammad read "wa-law yaqūlu ʿalaynā" with the ya' and a damma on the qāf; this reading is an allusion (taʿrīḍ) to what the reading of the majority states explicitly, and the allusion is clarified by His saying "ʿalaynā baʿḍa al-aqāwīl" (some sayings against Us).

As for His saying "La-akhadhnā minhu bil-yamīn" (We would have seized him by the right hand), its meaning has been disputed. Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "bil-yamīn" means "with power," and the meaning is: We would have reached His punishment with power from Us; or the meaning is: We would have taken away his strength. Others said it is an expression for humiliation, as one says of someone who is imprisoned or set up for punishment: "He has taken him by the hand and by the right hand."

"Al-Waṭīn" is the sinews of the heart (niyāṭ al-qalb), as Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, said. It is a thick vein that the blade of the slaughterer meets. From it is the saying of al-Shammākh:

"When you carry me and load my saddle to ʿArāba, then choke with the blood of the waṭīn."

So the meaning of the verse: We would have hastened to take away his life. "Al-ḥājiz" is the preventer, and the plural "ḥājizīn" is in consideration of the meaning of "aḥad" (anyone), since it applies to the plural; similar to His peace and blessings be upon him saying: "Spoils were not made lawful for anyone before you except the heads (ruʾūs)."

The pronoun in His saying "wa-innahu la-tadhkiratun" (and indeed, it is a reminder) refers to the Qur'an, and it was said that it refers to Muḥammad (ﷺ). His saying "wa-innā la-naʿlamu anna minkum mukadhdhibīn" (and indeed, We know that among you are deniers) is a warning (waʿīd). Its being a regret for the disbelievers is from the standpoint that they disbelieved, and they see that whoever believed in it is blessed while they are punished.

As for His saying "wa-innahu la-ḥaqqu al-yaqīn" (and indeed, it is the certain truth), the Kufans held that it is an idāfa of a thing to itself, like "dār al-ākhira" and "masjid al-jāmiʿ." The Basrans and the skilled grammarians held that "ḥaqq" is idāfa to the most eloquent of its aspects. Al-Mubarrad said: it is only like your saying "ʿayn al-yaqīn" and "maḥḍ al-yaqīn."

Then Allah the Exalted commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to glorify the name of his great Lord, and within that is persistence in his message, proceeding to perform and convey it. It is narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said when this verse was revealed: "Make it in your ruku'." A group of scholars recommended adhering to this, while Mālik disliked making it obligatory, lest it be regarded as an obligatory duty.

The commentary of Surah [al-Ḥāqqa] is complete, and praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds.
